name: Crowbar
popularity: 474 stars, 38 forks. No notable adoption cited; niche corporate-proxy-bypass tool.
maturity: Archived by owner May 21, 2025 (read-only), migrated to Codeberg. Only 29 commits total, minimal ongoing history. Explicitly labeled EXPERIMENTAL by author with known bugs (no rate limiting, descriptor/memory leaks) never fixed. Major red flag: dead project.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN. No admin/root required. Single Go binary (crowbar-forward); honors HTTP_PROXY env var. Simple to run but is a generic TCP-over-HTTP proxy client, not a public-URL reverse tunnel client.
server_requirements: Source available (Go), config-file-driven only (plaintext userfile of username:password pairs). No REST/HTTP API for programmatic tunnel registration; server just proxies arbitrary TCP tunnels to authenticated users, not per-tunnel public URLs.
has_programmable_api: false — no API; CLI/config-file only, and per-tunnel model doesn't match a hosted reverse-tunnel-to-localhost use case.
viability_notes: Wrong tool for the job: Crowbar tunnels arbitrary TCP over HTTP GET/POST to bypass restrictive proxies (e.g. SSH-over-HTTP), it does not expose a localhost service via a public subdomain/URL. Combined with being archived/abandoned and having no data confidentiality guarantees, this is a clear disqualification.

name: tunelo
popularity: 429 stars, 20 forks, 2 watchers. Markets itself as 'faster than frp, cloudflared, ngrok'; no other notable adoption evidence found.
maturity: Active repo (43 commits, main branch), has CI workflows, Docker/compose support, and a dedicated website (tunelo.net). No explicit last-commit date surfaced but repo structure (Cargo workspace, protocol/relay/tunelo crates) looks well organized and current. No obvious red flags beyond being a young/small project.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN. No admin/root needed — client is a single ~4MB Rust binary using QUIC (quinn+rustls) for the tunnel transport; `tunelo port <PORT>` just makes an outbound QUIC connection to the relay.
server_requirements: Source available (Rust, 'relay' crate). Self-hostable via `tunelo relay --domain yourdomain.com` or Docker image. Config/CLI-flag driven (--domain, --tunnel-addr, --http-addr); no documented HTTP/REST control-plane API for programmatic tunnel registration from an external app.
has_programmable_api: false — no REST/control-plane API documented; relay is started via CLI flags/env, tunnels are created by the client binary itself, not by a separate registration call.
viability_notes: Meets the hard client constraints well (no TUN, no root, single binary, cross-platform including Windows) and the relay/server is open source and self-hostable as a single binary too. However there is no programmable HTTP API or JS/TS SDK for our SvelteKit app to register/manage tunnels — we'd have to shell out to the CLI or build glue around process management ourselves.

name: mmar
popularity: 312 stars, 12 forks, 2 watchers. Public mmar.dev free service; documented in author's devlog series. Modest adoption.
maturity: Active — 129 commits, GoReleaser CI, Homebrew tap, Docker images published up to v0.2.6+. No clear red flags on maintenance, but functionally limited (see below).
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN, no admin/root needed at runtime (install script uses sudo only to place the binary in PATH). Zero-dependency single Go binary; Docker image also available. Simple `mmar client --local-port PORT`.
server_requirements: Source available (Go), self-hostable via Docker/compose with env-var config (USERNAME_HASH/PASSWORD_HASH, ports). Config/env-driven only — no HTTP/REST control-plane API for programmatic tunnel registration.
viability_notes: Client-side constraints are satisfied (no TUN, no root, single binary) but mmar explicitly states it 'currently only supports the HTTP protocol' and that 'websockets were not tested and will likely not work' — a serious problem for an inference server that likely needs streaming/websocket support. AGPL-3.0 licensing and lack of any programmatic API are further downsides.

name: remotemoe
popularity: 302 stars, 33 forks, 6 watchers. Public remote.moe test instance monitored via UptimeRobot (linked status badge implies real-world usage).
maturity: Active, mature — 141 commits, Go Report Card + uptime badges in README, ongoing infrastructure config in-repo (systemd unit template). No red flags; described candidly as 'not a SaaS' with no guarantees on the public instance.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN, no admin/root, and literally no software install at all — the 'client' is just the OS-provided ssh binary doing `ssh -R 80:localhost:PORT remotemoe-host`. This is about as install-free/admin-free as it gets.
server_requirements: Source available (Go). Server is an SSH daemon plus HTTP(S) reverse-proxy component that multiplexes tunnels by SNI/Host header; must run on port 22 (openssh must be moved aside). Entirely config/SSH-session driven — no REST/HTTP control-plane API for registering or managing tunnels programmatically; management happens via an interactive SSH shell (help/firsttime commands).
has_programmable_api: false — no HTTP API; control is via SSH protocol/interactive shell only, though this could in principle be scripted by spawning ssh processes from Node.
viability_notes: Best-in-class on the client side (zero install, zero admin, uses only the standard SSH client) and server source is available in Go, but there's no HTTP/REST control plane to hit from SvelteKit — our glue code would need to manage SSH keys/processes/config via the interactive SSH admin shell instead of an API, and it must bind to port 22 on the server.

name: docker-tunnel
license: Not specified (no LICENSE file found in repo listing)
popularity: 292 stars, 52 forks, 7 watchers, but only 1 contributor and no releases published — a small personal-blog-post project.
maturity: Abandoned: last commit Jul 6, 2019, only 10 commits total, no releases. Clear red flag — unmaintained for 6+ years.
client_requirements: Requires Docker installed on the client/dev machine plus mounting an SSH private key into the container (`docker run ... -v ~/.ssh/id_rsa:/ssh.key`). No TAP/TUN, but Docker itself is a nontrivial install and typically needs elevated/daemon privileges — fails the 'no complex install' bar.
server_requirements: Source available (shell scripts + nginx.conf.template + Dockerfile) but is purely a docker-run/env-var config wrapper around SSH reverse tunneling + nginx; no REST/HTTP API for programmatic registration.
viability_notes: Clear disqualification: unmaintained since 2019, no license file, and requires Docker (plus SSH key mounting) on the client side, which conflicts with the 'simple install, no complex setup' constraint. Not worth further investigation.

name: EXPOSE (exposesh/expose-server, renamed to gaetanlhf/EXPOSE)
language: Multi-component: Python (SSH server), Node.js (tools service), OpenResty/Nginx (web/proxy)
popularity: 293 stars, 6 forks, 2 watchers. Repo has been renamed/moved from exposesh/expose-server to gaetanlhf/EXPOSE (original URL redirects). Notable gimmick: requires starring the repo to gain access, which caps genuine independent adoption signals.
maturity: Active — 32 commits, includes demo video, deployed globally on Fly.io. No obvious staleness red flags, but the project is fairly young/small and tightly coupled to GitHub identity/Fly.io infra.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN, no admin/root, and no install at all — client is just the OS ssh binary: `ssh -R 1:localhost:3000 expose.sh`. Excellent on pure client simplicity.
server_requirements: Source available across 3 containerized components (SSH server in Python, 'Tools Service' in Node.js, web server via OpenResty/Nginx), deployable via Fly.io. Config is via fly.toml + env vars (HTTP_URL, SSH_SERVER_URL, GITHUB_REPOSITORY, etc.) — no documented public HTTP/REST API for third-party apps to register tunnels; the Node.js Tools Service is an internal intermediary (GitHub API caching, QR codes), not an external control-plane API.
has_programmable_api: false for external registration — there IS an internal Node.js service, but it's not exposed as a public API for programmatic tunnel management; auth/identity is hardwired to GitHub SSH keys + repo-star gating, incompatible with our own glue-code registration model.
viability_notes: Client side is ideal (zero install/admin, plain ssh), and there is a Node.js server component, but the whole system is architecturally tied to GitHub account identity and repo-starring for authorization rather than an API we control, and there's no exposed control-plane endpoint for programmatic registration. AGPL-3.0 and a 3-service deployment (Python+Node+Nginx on Fly.io) also add operational complexity for a self-hosted binary use case.

name: tunwg
popularity: 287 stars, 21 forks, 8 watchers. Public tunwg.com hosted instance; positioned as an ngrok alternative.
maturity: Active — 18 commits, CI workflows, devcontainer, Docker images published to ghcr.io. Self-describes remaining future work (e.g. distributed servers) but no red flags; server is explicitly stateless/simple.
client_requirements: CONFIRMED: does NOT need a TUN/TAP device or admin/root. Despite being 'WireGuard-userspace-based,' tunwg runs its own userspace TCP/IP stack via gVisor netstack and speaks WireGuard purely over a UDP socket in-process — no kernel WireGuard interface, no elevated privileges. Ships as a single Go binary (or Docker image with --network=host) for Linux/Mac/Windows.
server_requirements: Source available (Go). Self-hostable via `go install` + env vars (TUNWG_RUN_SERVER, TUNWG_API, TUNWG_IP, TUNWG_PORT, TUNWG_AUTH) or Docker; server is fully stateless (no DB), listens on 80/443 + a UDP WireGuard port. No HTTP/REST control-plane API for external tunnel registration — it's env/config driven. However it does offer a Go library API: `tunwg.NewListener(name)` returns a net.Listener usable directly in a Go program.
has_programmable_api: partial/true for Go only — `tunwg.NewListener()` is a real programmatic Go API for embedding tunnel creation directly into a Go server process; no JS/TS SDK and no HTTP control-plane API for cross-language/registration-style use from SvelteKit.
viability_notes: Strongest client-side fit in this batch: no TUN device despite being WireGuard-based, no root, single small binary, persistent URLs, built-in auto-TLS. Server is open source, stateless, and simple to self-host as a single binary. The only gap versus a 5 is the lack of an HTTP/REST or JS/TS control-plane API — the closest thing is a Go-only embeddable listener API, so our SvelteKit app would still need to shell out to the CLI or env-configure a fixed relay rather than hit a REST endpoint.

name: pgrok (jerson/pgrok)
license: Inherited from ngrok fork (original ngrok v1/v2 was Apache-2.0); repo shows a generic 'License' link, not independently re-verified
popularity: 284 stars, 56 forks, 1 watcher, 457 commits (mostly inherited ngrok history). Was used as a free ngrok alternative via the public ejemplo.me domain.
maturity: Archived by owner Dec 17, 2022 (read-only). README itself notes 'ejemplo.me service is shutting down.' Clear red flag: dead/unmaintained public instance and repo archived.
client_requirements: No TAP/TUN, no admin/root. Single binary installable via Homebrew (`brew install jerson/tap/pgrok`) or direct download, classic ngrok-style client (`pgrok -subdomain=x 3000`).
server_requirements: Source available (Go, forked from ngrok). Self-hostable server (`pgrokd`) via Homebrew or Docker Hub image, configured via CLI flags (-domain, -httpAddr, -httpsAddr, -tunnelAddr, -tlsCrt/-tlsKey). Includes a web inspection UI (127.0.0.1:4040) but no documented REST/HTTP control-plane API for external programmatic tunnel registration.
has_programmable_api: false — CLI/flag-configured only; local web inspector UI is for traffic inspection/replay, not tunnel registration.
viability_notes: Client/server install are both simple (Homebrew/Docker, no TUN/root), matching classic ngrok ergonomics, but the project has been archived since 2022 with its reference public service already shut down — a clear maintenance red flag for a production dependency. No programmable API is offered either.
